items.article: Reporter Will Puckett says he may never sign up to witness another execution after what happened to Christa Pike, but he has no regrets about being there. Puckett, the morning co-anchor for WVLT-TV in Knoxville, Tenn ., was one of seven journalists selected to bear witness to the execution of Christa Pike , who remains alive and in critical condition despite being administered two doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday. "When you agree to be a state-selected witness to an event like this, you know there's the possibility that you'll be called upon to walk people through the events that could be traumatic," Puckett told As It Happens host Nil Köksal. "And that's exactly where we're at today, is just relaying how the state of Tennessee failed to execute Christa Gail Pike appropriately and properly." Pike, 50, was 18 in January 1995 when she, her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, and a third companion lured their classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her. Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing and were convicted of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death while Schipp, who was 17 at the time of the crime, was sentenced to life in prison. Years later, Pike expressed remorse for what she'd done. Her lawyers and supporters tried to secure a stay of execution, citing her age at the time of the crime, mental health issues and a history of severe childhood neglect and sexual abuse.

items.article: An INTERPOL executive warns AI is making existing cyber threats faster and harder to detect, while companies face new risks from the rise of agentic AI. Artificial intelligence enables cyber threats by enhancing existing criminal tactics such as scams and fraud, according to INTERPOL. AI is enhancing existing criminal techniques rather than revolutionizing them, Bjorn R. Watne, global chief information security officer at INTERPOL, told CNBC on the sidelines of Tech Week Singapore on Thursday. Scam operators can use AI to target multiple victims simultaneously, while improved translation and digital identities are making it increasingly difficult to distinguish fraudulent interactions from real ones. "It's an evolution and not a revolution," Watne said, adding that AI is primarily increasing the "speed and scale" of existing techniques. As cyber threats evolve, companies should prioritize protective actions, according to Watne. Instead, businesses should first identify their "crown jewels," the assets most critical to keeping their operations running, and determine who would be most interested in stealing or disrupting them. They can then use threat intelligence to understand the tactics and technologies used by those adversaries and tailor their defenses accordingly.

items.text: Why oil is still trading near $100 even though Gulf exports have recovered
items.article: Persian Gulf oil exports rebounded to their 2025 average after doubling in September. Oil exports from the Persian Gulf have largely recovered to their 2025 average levels, but oil prices remain stubbornly high. On Thursday, international benchmark Brent crude oil futures were trading around $97 a barrel after surging during the Iran war, when attacks on energy infrastructure and fears of disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz rattled global oil markets. The recovery in Gulf oil exports has outpaced the decline in oil prices, according to analysts at Goldman Sachs in a note published on Tuesday. Goldman estimates Persian Gulf oil exports reached 23.3 million barrels a day over the past week, roughly matching their 2025 average after doubling in September. Higher shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, including ship-to-ship transfers, drove much of the recovery. That came despite a drone attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline last month and the Houthis' continuing blockade of Saudi exports through the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Saudi Arabia led the recovery, with exports rising above their 2025 average after shipments were redirected to eastern ports, Goldman's analysts wrote. Meanwhile, Iranian exports fell to below 20% of their 2025 average.

Heart disease is the leading cause of death among women in the United States, and more than 60 million U.S. women are living with some form of heart disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Growing research suggests that a test millions of women already receive to screen for breast cancer may also offer an important window into their heart health. Routine mammograms can show breast arterial calcifications (BACs), which are calcium deposits in the vessels of the breast. BACs are not related to breast cancer, but research shows women with BACs on their mammograms could double the risk of having a cardiovascular event such as a heart attack or a stroke . “BACs can be a woman’s first sign of heart disease,” Dr. Nisha Parikh, director of cardiovascular disease at the Katz Institute of Women’s Health at Northwell Health in New York City, told ABC News. Breast arterial calcifications are calcium deposits that can appear as bright lines on a mammogram. They are different from the usual calcifications radiologists evaluate when looking for signs of breast cancer.

As FZ1073 cruised at around 34,000 feet, the aircraft suddenly began losing altitude, plunging more than 14,000 feet in less than a minute. At the same time, the captain was reportedly attacked and stabbed by his co-pilot. Despite being seriously injured, Captain Smit Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, creating an opportunity for passengers and crew to intervene. Passengers rushed forward, helped overpower the attacker and secured the cockpit. Off-duty pilots travelling on the flight then took control of the aircraft and began the process of stabilising and diverting it. The Flydubai cockpit horror is being described as an extraordinary fight for control, with the captain's presence of mind and the passengers' quick response playing a crucial role in saving the aircraft.
